title: 3SUM Is Really Hard: A Real-to-Integer Reduction

paper.title: 3SUM Is Really Hard: A Real-to-Integer Reduction
paper.abstract: Abstract We show that if the 3SUM problem on integer-valued inputs can be solved in truly subquadratic time, then it can also be solved in truly subquadratic time on real-valued inputs. This answers an open problem posed by Chan, Vassilevska Williams, and Xu [STOC 2022], and constitutes the first such tight real-to-integer self-reduction in fine-grained complexity. Our proof relies on a surprising combination of the Frank–Tardos theorem from optimization with Freiman-type theorems from additive combinatorics.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Given n n numbers, the 3SUM problem asks whether any three of them sum up to zero. It can be solved in time O ⁡ ( n 2 ) O(n^{2}) . One of the three main hypotheses of fine-grained complexity [ 39 ] , the 3SUM Hypothesis , asserts that this running time is optimal, up to subpolynomial n o ⁡ ( 1 ) n^{o(1)} factors. Some mild polylogarithmic improvements over the quadratic running time are however possible. In particular, Baran, Demaine and Pătra s , cu [ 2 ] showed that relatively simple hashing and bit-packing tricks suffice to obtain an O ⁡ ( n 2 log 2 ⁡ n ​ polyloglog ⁡ ( n ) ) O\big(\frac{n^{2}}{\log^{2}n}\polyloglog(n)\big) -time algorithm for Integer 3SUM, i.e., 3SUM with input numbers required to be integers. It took much more time and a series of papers [ 28 , 25 , 23 , 10 ] to arrive at the same running time also for real-valued inputs, and these Real 3SUM algorithms employ a significantly more complex approach based on linear decision trees. Gajentaan and Overmars [ 24 ] first introduced 3SUM in the context of conditional lower bounds for computational geometry problems, where it is natural to consider real-valued inputs. Later, Pătra s , cu [ 34 ] showed how to use hashing to reduce Integer 3SUM to combinatorial problems, such as finding triangles in graphs. This technique has quickly become prevalent in 3SUM-based hardness proofs (see [ 17 ] ), and in modern fine-grained complexity, 3SUM is essentially synonymous with Integer 3SUM. Chan, Vassilevska Williams, and Xu [ 7 ] asked whether fine-grained reductions from Integer 3SUM can be turned into reductions from Real 3SUM, and they made a partial progress on this question. In particular, they give non-tight reductions from Real 3SUM to the Integer All-Numbers 3SUM, All-Color-Pairs Triangle Collection, All-Edges Sparse Triangle, and All-Edges Monochromatic Triangle problems, as well as tight reductions to counting versions of the last two problems. They remark that “(…) it would be extremely interesting if one could show that the Real 3SUM hypothesis implies the Integer 3SUM hypothesis.” Our main result establishes this implication. 1.1 Real-to-Integer Reduction for 3SUM. If Integer 3SUM can be solved in time O ⁡ ( n 2 − ϵ ) O(n^{2-\epsilon}) , for some constant ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 , then Real 3SUM can be solved in time O ⁡ ( n 2 − Ω ⁡ ( ϵ 4 ) ) O(n^{2-\Omega(\epsilon^{4})}) (in the comparison-addition model). In other words, we show that Integer 3SUM is as hard as Real 3SUM. Thus, if we believe that Real 3SUM is really hard, then also Integer 3SUM and all the numerous problems with known (Integer) 3SUM-based fine-grained lower bounds are also really hard. We consider this result quite unexpected. To our knowledge, it constitutes the first and only tight real-to-integer self-reduction in fine-grained algorithms and complexity. Our result fits a broader line of work that tries to understand how much of the hashing-based machinery developed around 3SUM (and other related problems such as Subset Sum) is actually necessary. One part of this line deals with derandomization [ 5 , 17 ] , another (including this work) with real-valued inputs [ 7 , 19 ] .

sections.heading: Further Consequences.
sections.text: Our reduction from Real to Integer 3SUM goes through an intermediate problem, the Real Convolution 3SUM problem, which asks, for a given input sequence a ∈ ℝ n a\in\mathbb{R}^{n} , to determine if there exist i , j , k i,j,k such that i + j = k i+j=k and a ⁡ [ i ] + a ⁡ [ j ] = a ⁡ [ k ] a[i]+a[j]=a[k] . The integer-valued version of this problem was first introduced by Pătra s , cu [ 34 ] , who showed that it is equivalent to Integer 3SUM under subquadratic fine-grained reductions, and used it as an intermediate problem for showing hardness of a number of combinatorial problems. Pătra s , cu’s reduction from 3SUM to Convolution 3SUM relies on linear hashing as in [ 2 ] —a technique inherently only suited to integers. It was later simplified and derandomized by Chan and He [ 5 ] , who “leave open the question of whether (…) a similar reduction from 3SUM to Convolution 3SUM is possible for real numbers.” We answer this question in the affirmative with our intermediate reduction ( Theorem 4.1 ). Another important problem in fine-grained complexity is the Exact Triangle problem, which asks to determine whether a given edge-weighted graph contains a triangle whose total edge weight equals exactly zero. In the world of integer-valued inputs, Exact Triangle is known to be harder than both 3SUM [ 41 ] and APSP [ 40 ] (All-Pairs Shortest Path, the second of the three central problems in fine-grained complexity), and thus its conjectured hardness gives rise to a weaker unifying hypothesis, which turns out to be sufficient to prove hardness of many problems previously known to be 3SUM-hard [ 42 , 9 ] . Up until now it was not known if there is a real analogue of the reduction from (Integer) 3SUM to (Integer) Exact Triangle. This reduction goes through the Convolution 3SUM problem and applies a generic convolution-to-product transformation [ 41 ] —the latter would work as well with real-valued inputs, but only our Theorem 4.1 establishes a real counterpart of the former. 1.2 . If Real Exact Triangle can be solved in time O ⁡ ( n 2 − ϵ ) O(n^{2-\epsilon}) , for some constant ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 , then Real 3SUM can be solved in time O ⁡ ( n 2 − Ω ⁡ ( ϵ 2 ) ) O(n^{2-\Omega(\epsilon^{2})}) (in the comparison-addition model). Another immediate consequence of our result is that all problems previously known to be as hard as Integer 3SUM (e.g., All-Pairs Sparse Triangle [ 34 , 31 ] ) are now also known to be as hard as Real 3SUM.

sections.heading: 1.1 Computational Model
sections.text: In fine-grained complexity it is customary work in the word RAM model of computation with O ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) O(\log n) -bit words, which is a natural choice when the input consists of polynomially bounded integers. However, to deal with real-valued inputs, we need to move to a real RAM model with dedicated registers for storing real numbers and performing specific operations on them. Here we need to be particularly careful when describing the set of allowed operations on these real numbers, because reals are inherently infinite-precision and thus the model can easily gain unreasonable computational power. For instance, it is known that when supporting infinite-precision arithmetic operations and flooring allows solving PSPACE-complete problems in polynomial time [ 29 ] . But even without flooring, the real RAM model is unexpectedly powerful. The fine-grained complexity landscape would look very differently in that model; for instance, computing all-pairs shortest paths (in graphs with integer edge weights) is in truly subcubic time [ 44 ] . While 3SUM with real-valued input may still require quadratic time in such an unreasonably powerful computational model, we prefer to state our reductions in a model as weak as possible. It turns out that our reduction can be implemented in a very weak model, the comparison-addition model. This model, on top of the word RAM model, supports only two real-valued operations: comparisons ( a < b a<b ) and additions—no multiplication, no flooring, no logarithms. In fact, our reduction works in an even more restricted model which we will refer to as the realistic comparison-addition model. This model supports only a single operation, namely to evaluate a comparison of the form ∑ i = 1 m n i ​ α i ≥ 0 , \sum_{i=1}^{m}n_{i}\alpha_{i}\geq 0, where the n i n_{i} ’s are arbitrary non-zero integers and the α i \alpha_{i} ’s are input reals; each such operation is assumed to take time ( ∑ i = 1 m log ⁡ | n i | ) O ⁡ ( 1 ) (\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log|n_{i}|)^{O(1)} . 1 1 1 Note that we can still simulate additions in the realistic comparison-addition model, by performing all additions symbolically . Concretely, define a symbolic number as a tuple ( n 1 , … , n m , α 1 , … , α m ) (n_{1},\dots,n_{m},\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{m}) representing ∑ i = 1 m n i ​ α i \sum_{i=1}^{m}n_{i}\alpha_{i} , where the n i n_{i} ’s are integers and the α i \alpha_{i} ’s are pointers to the input reals. Two symbolic numbers can be added in time ( ∑ i = 1 m log ⁡ | n i | ) O ⁡ ( 1 ) (\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log|n_{i}|)^{O(1)} without invoking any operations on reals. Only a comparison of two symbolic numbers becomes one operation in the realistic comparison-addition model. One can similarly simulate subtractions and multiplications/divisions by integers. Note that this is exactly the time it would take to evaluate the comparison in the word RAM model if the α i \alpha_{i} ’s were polynomially-bounded integers. In this sense, the realistic comparison-addition model is a safe choice, as it must inherit the same fine-grained complexity landscape as the word RAM model for integer inputs. It is possible to impose further restrictions on the model (such as further restricting the number of terms in each sum); we refer to [ 7 , Appendix A in the arXiv version] for a deeper discussion. Curiously, the only reason why we cannot show that Integer 3SUM is equivalent to Real 3SUM in the comparison-addition model is that the simple direction, reducing Integer 3SUM to Real 3SUM, does not work. After all, a hypothetical O ⁡ ( n 2 − ϵ ) O(n^{2-\epsilon}) -time algorithm for Real 3SUM in the comparison-addition model might somehow rely on the unbounded power of the model (e.g., by constructing huge numbers with repeated squaring), and may for this reason not be transferable in the word RAM model. In contrast, the realistic comparison-addition model can be simulated by the word RAM model. For this reason, we do obtain the anticipated equivalence in the realistic comparison-addition model: 1.3 Equivalence. Integer 3SUM can be solved in the word RAM model in time O ⁡ ( n 2 − ϵ ) O(n^{2-\epsilon}) , for some constant ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 , if and only if Real 3SUM can be solved in the realistic comparison-addition model in time O ⁡ ( n 2 − ϵ ′ ) O(n^{2-\epsilon^{\prime}}) , for some constant ϵ ′ > 0 \epsilon^{\prime}>0 .

sections.heading: 1.2 Technical Overview
sections.text: In this section, we describe the high-level ideas behind our real-to-integer reduction. It differs fundamentally from the previous non-tight reduction of Chan, Vassilevska Williams, and Xu [ 7 ] . Their proof is built around the All-Edges Sparse Triangle problem, which asks to identify all edges that participate in triangles in a given sparse graph. This problem is known to admit a tight reduction from (Integer) 3SUM [ 34 , 31 ] , as well as a simple non-tight reduction to 3SUM. One of the main results of [ 7 ] is to extend the former reduction to reals, establishing a non-tight reduction from Real 3SUM to All-Edges Sparse Triangle. 2 2 2 Notably, as a direct corollary of Theorem 1.1 , we obtain a tight reduction from Real 3SUM to All-Edges Sparse Triangle. By transitivity, this yields a non-tight reduction from Real 3SUM to 3SUM. This is a conceptually clean approach, but it seems unlikely to yield a tight reduction as in Theorem 1.1 . A major obstacle is that APSP is also known to admit a tight reduction to All-Edges Sparse Triangle [ 42 , 7 ] . Consequently, a tight reduction along these lines would also imply a tight connection between 3SUM and APSP—a major open question in fine-grained complexity. For this reason, we depart entirely from this framework, and start over from scratch. Let A ⊆ ℝ A\subseteq\mathbb{R} denote a Real 3SUM instance. Perhaps the most basic and naive idea is to aim for a simple mapping from A A to an equivalent set of integers. Concretely, does there exist a function h : A → ℤ h:A\to\mathbb{Z} such that a + b + c = 0 ​ if and only if ​ h ​ ( a ) + h ⁡ ( b ) + h ⁡ ( c ) = 0 ​ ? a+b+c=0\;\;\text{if and only if}\;\;h(a)+h(b)+h(c)=0? (1) And if so, can it be computed efficiently? With access to such a function h h , the reduction would be trivial: simply replace A A by the equivalent Integer 3SUM instance { h ⁡ ( a ) : a ∈ A } \{h(a):a\in A\} . To our initial surprise, the short answer is: yes, essentially! The detailed answer involves four interesting ideas.

sections.heading: Idea 1: Frank–Tardos Theorem
sections.text: The first idea, and our starting point, is to exploit the celebrated Frank–Tardos theorem [ 20 ] from optimization. In its original form, it states that any 0–1 optimization problem can be solved in polynomial time if and only it can be solved in strongly 3 3 3 Informally, an algorithm with integer inputs is said to run in strongly polynomial time if it runs in polynomial time, and performs only arithmetic operations ( + , − , ⋅ , / {+},{-},{\cdot},{/} ) and comparisons ( = , ≤ , ≥ , < , > ) ({=},{\leq},{\geq},{<},{>}) on the integer inputs (and no other operations such as flooring). In particular, all intermediate results are integers that can be stored in polynomial space. polynomial time. The key technical claim is as follows, intuitively stating that any set of reals can be replaced by (large) integers so that the order of its subset sums is preserved. 1.4 Frank–Tardos [ 20 ] . There is an algorithm that, given reals α ∈ ℝ d \alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , runs in polynomial time d O ⁡ ( 1 ) d^{O(1)} and computes integers v ∈ ℤ d v\in\mathbb{Z}^{d} such that (i) ∥ v ∥ ∞ ≤ 2 O ⁡ ( d 3 ) \lVert v\rVert_{\infty}\leq 2^{O(d^{3})} , and (ii) α T ​ x ≥ 0 \alpha^{T}x\geq 0 if and only if v T ​ x ≥ 0 v^{T}x\geq 0 , for all x ∈ { − 1 , 0 , 1 } d x\in\{-1,0,1\}^{d} . Although our setting differs from that considered by Frank and Tardos, it turns out that this theorem is similarly valid in the comparison-addition model for computing with reals. In Section 3.1 we retrace the proof of Theorem 1.4 , following the beautiful exposition by Eisenbrand [ 15 ] , to verify that all required operations on reals can be implemented as claimed. Returning to our earlier question, Theorem 1.4 directly entails the existence of the desired function h h . Indeed, let α 1 , … , α n \alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n} denote the elements of A A , and apply the theorem with d = n d=n to obtain integers v 1 , … , v n v_{1},\dots,v_{n} . Then take the function h h defined by h ⁡ ( α i ) = v i h(\alpha_{i})=v_{i} ; Theorem 1.4 implies condition ( 1 ) (as it implies both the ≥ \geq and ≤ \leq variants of this equivalence). This is an encouraging starting point, but a fundamental obstacle remains: the Frank–Tardos algorithm is far too slow. It builds on top of the LLL lattice reduction algorithm [ 32 ] , which itself already runs in time O ⁡ ( d 6 ) O(d^{6}) , and introduces some more polynomial factors along the way. For d = n d=n , this yields a running time of O ⁡ ( n 6 ) O(n^{6}) , which is well beyond the subquadratic budget n 2 − Ω ⁡ ( 1 ) n^{2-\Omega(1)} required for our reduction. Even worse, it is unconditionally impossible to improve the running time of Theorem 1.4 to subquadratic, since the output size is necessarily Ω ⁡ ( d 2 ) \Omega(d^{2}) . 4 4 4 To see this, let α \alpha be the length- 2 ​ d 2d vector where the first d d entries are defined by α i = 2 i \alpha_{i}=2^{i} and the last d d entries consist of arbitrary integers α d + 1 , … , a 2 ​ d \alpha_{d+1},\dots,a_{2d} in the range [ 0 , 2 d − 1 ] [0,2^{d}-1] . Let v v denote the integer vector implied by Theorem 1.4 . Then one can exactly reconstruct α d + 1 , … , a 2 ​ d \alpha_{d+1},\dots,a_{2d} from v v . Indeed, the bit-representation of α i \alpha_{i} is the unique vector b ∈ { 0 , 1 } d b\in\{0,1\}^{d} such that ∑ j = 1 d v j ​ b j = v i \sum_{j=1}^{d}v_{j}b_{j}=v_{i} . It takes Ω ⁡ ( d 2 ) \Omega(d^{2}) bits to specify α d + 1 , … , a 2 ​ d \alpha_{d+1},\dots,a_{2d} , and thus also Ω ⁡ ( d 2 ) \Omega(d^{2}) bits to specify v v . Overcoming this issue is our key challenge in this paper. Our proposed solution is new and conceptually exciting, but technically quite involved. It relies on several more ideas to be described next.

sections.heading: Idea 2: Subset Sum Covers
sections.text: Since applying the Frank–Tardos theorem to all n n input reals is too expensive, a natural strategy is to invoke it on a much smaller set, say for d = O ⁡ ( n 0.1 ) d=O(n^{0.1}) . In that case, the polynomial running time becomes subquadratic, which is within our time budget. To understand which restricted set of reals to use, observe that we have not fully exhausted the power of the Frank–Tardos theorem before: it not only preserves the order of 3-sums α i + α j + α k \alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j}+\alpha_{k} , but in fact of arbitrary subset sums α T ​ x \alpha^{T}x (for x ∈ { 0 , 1 } d x\in\{0,1\}^{d} ). Thus, to effectively use Theorem 1.4 it would be sufficient to have access to a vector α \alpha so that each element in A A can be expressed as a subset sum of α \alpha ; in this case we call α \alpha a subset sum cover of A A . We refer to the length of α \alpha as the rank of the subset sum cover. In this language, our goal is to find a rank- O ⁡ ( n 0.1 ) O(n^{0.1}) subset sum cover of A A . Unfortunately, such a low-rank subset sum cover might not exist—in fact, it typically does not exist! Any set A A without additive structure (e.g., a set of n n random reals in some prescribed range) does not admit subset sum covers of rank smaller than | A | |A| . Experience shows that these unstructured sets are likely among the hardest instances of 3SUM. Surprisingly, we still manage to make this approach work. Even if A A might not admit a low-rank subset sum cover, we show that an appropriate approximation of A A always does. Specifically, we show the following two statements: (a) any sufficiently additively structured set has an O ⁡ ( n 0.1 ) O(n^{0.1}) -rank subset sum cover, and (b) any Real 3SUM instance A A can be forced to become additively structured by appropriately rounding it. In what follows we describe our solutions to these two subgoals.

sections.heading: Idea 3: Additive Combinatorics and Freiman’s Theorem
sections.text: We begin with subgoal 1 . Suppose for now that A A is additively structured; we show that in this case one can efficiently construct a low-rank subset sum cover of A A . To formalize this, we must specify what “additively structured” means. Additive combinatorics offers several such notions, and we later make use of multiple variants. For the purposes of this overview, however, we focus on the most basic one: small doubling . Let A + B ≔ { a + b : a ∈ A , b ∈ B } A+B\coloneqq\{a+b:a\in A,b\in B\} denote the sumset of two sets A A and B B . The doubling of a set A A is defined as K ≔ | A + A | | A | . K\coloneqq\frac{|A+A|}{|A|}. This parameter ranges from 1 1 to | A | |A| . Highly structured sets (e.g., arithmetic progressions A = { a , 2 ​ a , … , n ​ a } A=\{a,2a,\dots,na\} ) have K = O ⁡ ( 1 ) K=O(1) , whereas unstructured sets (such as random sets) typically have K K close to | A | |A| . Our goal is thus to show that any low-doubling set admits a low-rank subset sum cover. This precisely concerns a central result in additive combinatorics, namely Freiman’s theorem. To state it, we introduce one more definition. A generalized arithmetic progression (GAP) of rank d d is a set of the form { α T ​ x : 0 ≤ x i ≤ N i } , \left\{\alpha^{T}x:0\leq x_{i}\leq N_{i}\right\}, for some α ∈ ℝ d \alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and N ∈ ℤ > 0 d N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{d} . This should be viewed as a generalized set of subset sums of α \alpha , where each item α i \alpha_{i} may be used up to N i N_{i} times. Freiman’s theorem [ 22 ] states that every low-doubling set is contained in a low-rank GAP. The following quantitative bounds are due to Ruzsa [ 36 ] and Chang [ 11 ] . 5 5 5 Historically, Freiman’s original proof [ 22 ] gave weaker quantitative bounds; see also [ 3 ] . Ruzsa later provided an alternative proof [ 36 ] , which was sharpened by Chang [ 11 ] to obtain the bounds in Theorem 1.5 . Some of these results are phrased for integers, but actually work for arbitrary torsion-free abelian groups, and were further generalized to arbitrary abelian groups by Ruzsa and Green [ 27 ] . Modern formulations often relax containment to covering by a few translates, yielding significantly improved bounds; see, e.g., the milestones [ 37 , 26 ] . 1.5 Freiman’s Theorem. Let A ⊆ ℝ A\subseteq\mathbb{R} be a set with doubling | A + A | ≤ K ​ | A | |A+A|\leq K|A| . Then A A is contained in a generalized arithmetic progression of size | A | ⋅ exp ⁡ ( K O ⁡ ( 1 ) ) |A|\cdot\exp(K^{O(1)}) and rank K O ⁡ ( 1 ) K^{O(1)} . Freiman’s theorem immediately implies that any set with doubling | A + A | ≤ K ​ | A | |A+A|\leq K|A| admits a subset sum cover of rank K O ⁡ ( 1 ) ​ log ⁡ | A | K^{O(1)}\log|A| . Indeed, Theorem 1.5 embeds A A into a GAP of rank d = K O ⁡ ( 1 ) d=K^{O(1)} . Then replace each item α i \alpha_{i} by α i , 2 ​ α i , … , 2 ⌈ log ⁡ N i ⌉ ​ α i \alpha_{i},2\alpha_{i},\dots,2^{\lceil\log N_{i}\rceil}\alpha_{i} , so that each multiple x i ⋅ α i x_{i}\cdot\alpha_{i} for 0 ≤ x i ≤ N i 0\leq x_{i}\leq N_{i} can be now be expressed as a subset sum. Consequently, the desired subset sum cover exists. But again, this argument is purely existential—we still require an efficient algorithm to construct such a cover. While algorithmic versions of Freiman’s theorem have been studied for integer sets [ 35 ] , extending them to real inputs introduces a substantial obstacle. A key step in proofs over the reals (and more generally torsion-free groups) is a modeling lemma , which replaces A ⊆ ℝ A\subseteq\mathbb{R} by an integer set A ′ ⊆ ℤ A^{\prime}\subseteq\mathbb{Z} with equivalent additive structure (a so-called Freiman-isomorphic set); see [ 38 , Lemma 5.25] . This lemma admits a simple non-constructive proof via the structure theorem for finitely-generated torsion-free groups [ 38 , Corollary 3.6] . But here we encounter a circularity: an algorithmic version of the modeling lemma essentially requires the Frank–Tardos theorem. But invoking Frank–Tardos is precisely what we sought to avoid, putting us back to square one. We follow a different approach. Instead, we devise a new, completely different, and much simpler proof of a weaker version of Freiman’s theorem: 1.6 Poor Man’s Freiman’s Theorem. Let A ⊆ ℝ A\subseteq\mathbb{R} be a set with doubling | A + A | ≤ K ​ | A | |A+A|\leq K|A| . Then A A has a subset sum cover of rank ( K ​ log ⁡ | A | ) O ⁡ ( 1 ) (K\log|A|)^{O(1)} . Really the only difference between Theorems 1.5 and 1.6 is that in Theorem 1.6 the rank is allowed to depend polynomially on log ⁡ | A | \log|A| (we omitted the size bound, but it could be guaranteed analogously). For us this dependence on log ⁡ | A | \log|A| is completely acceptable, as we typically think of K = O ⁡ ( | A | 0.1 ) K=O(|A|^{0.1}) , say. In contrast, typical additive combinatorics results try to avoid any overhead in terms of | A | |A| (thinking of K K as a doubling constant ). Our more coarse-grained perspective turns out to be a significant advantage here. In a nutshell, our proof of Theorem 1.6 is along the following lines. Any small-doubling set A A must have many popular differences, i.e., numbers x x that can be expressed in many ways as a 1 − a 2 = x a_{1}-a_{2}=x for a 1 , a 2 ∈ A a_{1},a_{2}\in A . To cover a 1 a_{1} we simply keep inserting popular differences into α \alpha . To analyze this process we think of an initial empty graph over the vertices A A . With each sampled popular difference we add some random edges ( a 1 , a 2 ) (a_{1},a_{2}) to the graph, symbolizing that once we cover one of the two endpoints, we automatically also cover the other endpoint. By an analysis akin to Borůvka’s algorithm for Minimum Spanning Tree [ 4 ] , we argue that after few samples, namely ( K ​ log ⁡ | A | ) O ⁡ ( 1 ) (K\log|A|)^{O(1)} , the graph becomes (almost) fully connected. Once that happens we can take an arbitrary root vertex a 0 ∈ A a_{0}\in A , add a 0 a_{0} to the subset sum cover, and thereby also cover all other vertices in the graph.

sections.heading: Idea 4: Forcing Additive Structure by Rounding
sections.text: So far we have described how to handle the case that the given Real 3SUM instance A A is additively structured. We now turn to subgoal 2 and show that we can always transform A A into an equivalent, but additively structured, set. At first glance, this may seem paradoxical. Indeed, several prior works show that 3SUM on additively structured instances can be solved in truly subquadratic time [ 6 , 1 , 30 , 18 , 16 ] . Thus, if we could simply enforce additive structure without further cost, we would refute the 3SUM Hypothesis outright. The crux is that the transformation necessarily introduces many false positives , that is, triples a , b , c ∈ A a,b,c\in A that are not solutions in the original instance but become solutions after the transformation. Consequently, it is not enough to solve the transformed instance—we must also efficiently enumerate and filter a large number of candidate solutions. This phenomenon is standard in 3SUM-based reductions. For example, a simple universe reduction maps any integer 3SUM instance to one over a bounded universe [ u ] [u] , but incurs O ⁡ ( n 3 / u ) O(n^{3}/u) false positives. Such reductions typically rely on integer-specific techniques, such as reducing all numbers modulo a random prime in [ u , 2 ​ u ] [u,2u] . The natural approach in the real setting is to round . To illustrate this idea, consider the following idealized scenario. Suppose there exists some Δ ∈ ℝ ≥ 0 \Delta\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} satisfying two properties: (i) the set A ^ \hat{A} , obtained from A A by rounding each element to its nearest integer multiple of Δ \Delta , is additively structured (e.g., | A ^ + A ^ | ≤ K ​ | A ^ | |\hat{A}+\hat{A}|\leq K|\hat{A}| for K = n 0.1 K=n^{0.1} ), and (ii) there are few false positives, | { ( a , b , c ) ∈ A 3 : a + b + c ≠ 0 , a + b + c = 0 ± Δ } | ≤ n 1.9 \lvert\{(a,b,c)\in A^{3}:a+b+c\neq 0,a+b+c=0\pm\Delta\}\rvert\leq n^{1.9} . This situation arises, for example, when A A consists of n n random reals in [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] . Indeed, for Δ ≈ n − 1.1 \Delta\approx n^{-1.1} , the number of false positives is O ⁡ ( n 1.9 ) O(n^{1.9}) . At the same time, A ^ + A ^ \hat{A}+\hat{A} has size at most O ⁡ ( n 1.1 ) O(n^{1.1}) (since there are only O ⁡ ( n 1.1 ) O(n^{1.1}) multiples of Δ \Delta in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] ), and hence A ^ \hat{A} has doubling O ⁡ ( n 0.1 ) O(n^{0.1}) . In this idealized setting, we can replace A A with A ^ \hat{A} . All true solutions are preserved (up to an additive offset of Δ \Delta or 2 ​ Δ 2\Delta ). By 1 , the set A ^ \hat{A} is additively structured, and we can therefore compute a subset sum cover using our “Poor Man’s” Freiman’s theorem. Applying the Frank–Tardos theorem to this cover yields the desired mapping h : A ^ → ℤ h:\hat{A}\to\mathbb{Z} . We thus obtain an integer instance { h ⁡ ( a ) : a ∈ A ^ } \{h(a):a\in\hat{A}\} that preserves all solutions, at the cost of introducing at most n 1.9 n^{1.9} false positives by 2 . Finally, these can be handled using the standard reduction from listing to decision: if Integer 3SUM can be solved in time O ⁡ ( n 2 − ϵ ) O(n^{2-\epsilon}) , then n 1.9 n^{1.9} solutions can be listed in time O ⁡ ( n 2 − ϵ ′ ) O(n^{2-\epsilon^{\prime}}) [ 40 ] (see Lemma 5.2 ). In this idealized regime, the real-to-integer reduction is complete. Unfortunately, the idealized setting overlooks two big problems.

sections.heading: Problem 1: Rounding
sections.text: The first obstacle is that we cannot explicitly construct A ^ \hat{A} in the comparison-addition model—or, in fact, in any “reasonable” model of real computation. Indeed, access to such a rounding primitive is known to enable polynomial-time algorithms even for PSPACE-complete problems [ 29 ] . To circumvent this, we avoid constructing A ^ \hat{A} altogether and instead work directly with A A and approximate solutions of the form a + b + c = 0 ± Δ a+b+c=0\pm\Delta . As a consequence, we need approximate versions of all necessary additive combinatorics statements (see Section 3.2 ), and an approximate version of subset sum covers and all related lemmas (see Section 3.3 ). This is mostly tedious, and we omit further details here.

sections.heading: Problem 2: Different Scales
sections.text: The more serious obstacle is that there may be no approximation threshold Δ \Delta that simultaneously satisfies Properties 1 and 2 . For example, consider a set A = { a 1 , … , a n } A=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\} whose elements lie at very different scales, say | a i | ∈ [ 2 i , 2 i + 1 ] |a_{i}|\in[2^{i},2^{i+1}] . For any choice of Δ \Delta , some elements (those with 2 i + 1 ≤ Δ 2^{i+1}\leq\Delta ) will participate in too many false positives, violating 2 , while for others (those with 2 i ≥ Δ 2^{i}\geq\Delta ) we have not introduced enough additive structure, violating 1 . Our solution is to manually separate these scales, i.e., to partition A A in a way so that each part contains only elements from roughly the same “scale”. Within each part we apply the previous machinery to perform the real-to-integer reduction. But we also need to detect solutions across different parts. Here we proceed differently, exploiting that the search space of solutions across different parts is highly restricted. In the example above, every 3SUM solution must be of the form a i + a j + a j + 1 = 0 a_{i}+a_{j}+a_{j+1}=0 , and all such solutions can be found in O ⁡ ( n ) O(n) time by enumerating j j . Turning this intuition into a formal argument is highly nontrivial and requires substantial effort. In particular, our approach does not yield a direct reduction from Real 3SUM to Integer 3SUM, but instead proceeds via an intermediate problem, namely Real Convolution 3SUM: • First, we reduce Real 3SUM to Real Convolution 3SUM using a coarse-grained rounding step. At this stage, the goal is not to tightly control false positives, but rather to identify convolution structure. Crucially, we thereby ensure that the total number of approximate solutions is at most n 2 n^{2} (before, there could have been up to n 3 n^{3} approximate solutions). See Section 4 for details, and in particular Lemma 4.3 , which is the key lemma underlying scale separation. • Second, we reduce Real Convolution 3SUM to Integer 3SUM via a more refined rounding step. Here we really need to keep the number of false positives small: smaller than the trivial upper bound of n 2 n^{2} (in contrast, a direct approach from 3SUM could incur up to n 3 n^{3} false positives now). See Section 5 for the details on how to separate scales. Another interesting trick we build on here is an analogue of “Fredman’s trick” [ 21 , 8 ] for convolutions; see the discussion in Section 5.5 .

sections.heading: 3 Real-to-Integer Toolkit
sections.text: In this section, we develop the tools that we will use throughout our reduction. We first restate the Frank–Tardos theorem and derive its implementation in the comparison-addition model (see Section 3.1 ). Next, we convert some definitions and lemmas from additive combinatorics into corresponding versions for approximate reals (see Section 3.2 ). Then, we define subset sum covers, show how to construct and use them in combination with Frank–Tardos, and prove our “Poor Man’s” Freiman’s theorem (see Section 3.3 ). sections.heading: 5 Reduction from Real Convolution 3SUM to Integer 3SUM
sections.text: In this section we give our reduction from Real Convolution 3SUM to Integer 3SUM. Together with Theorem 4.1 , this completes the proof of Theorem 1.1 . 5.1 . If Integer 3SUM can be solved in time O ⁡ ( n 2 − ϵ ) O(n^{2-\epsilon}) , for some constant ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 , then Real Convolution 3SUM can be solved in time O ⁡ ( n 2 − Ω ⁡ ( ϵ 2 ) ) O(n^{2-\Omega(\epsilon^{2})}) . On a high level, the proof proceeds by first rounding all numbers to a suitable scale, i.e., computing Δ \Delta such that we have many solutions up to ± Δ \pm\Delta , but not too many such that we can still list them. Then, in Section 5.3 , we split again into popular and unpopular elements, that is, elements participating in many and few solutions energy quadruples, and hence solutions due to Lemma 3.4 (for technical reasons, we also work with an intermediate, quasi-popular level). In Section 5.4 , we explain how to list approximate solutions where every element is at least quasi-popular using our machinery from Section 3 . To list solutions with both unpopular and popular elements, in Section 5.5 we develop a solution akin to Fredman’s trick [ 21 , 8 ] . Finally, in Section 5.6 , we can remove all popular elements from the instance, and repeat the whole algorithm until every element was popular for at least one Δ \Delta or the number of triples left is small enough to list all of them. In Sections 5.1 and 5.2 , we state two more necessary tools for the proof: a listing-to-decision reduction for 3SUM, and an equivalent version of Real Convolution 3SUM that we work with.

sections.heading: 5.1 Listing-to-Decision Reduction for 3SUM
sections.text: In this section we argue that if (the decision variant of) Integer 3SUM can be solved in subquadratic time, then it is also possible to list any subquadratic number of solutions in subquadratic time. This proof mostly follows standard arguments [ 40 , 14 ] , but to get exactly the bound we need, we cannot reuse them in a black-box manner, and we need to prove the following lemma. 5.2 Listing-to-Decision Reduction for 3SUM. Assume that there is a decision algorithm for Integer 3SUM running in time O ⁡ ( n 2 − ε ) O(n^{2-\varepsilon}) , for some ε > 0 \varepsilon>0 . Then there is also an algorithm that, given three size- n n sets of integers A , B , C A,B,C , and a number T T , lists up to T T solution triples ( a , b , c ) ∈ A × B × C (a,b,c)\in A\times B\times C with a + b + c = 0 a+b+c=0 in time O ⁡ ( n 2 − ε ​ T ε / 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) O(n^{2-\varepsilon}T^{\varepsilon/2}\log n) . For each of the three input sets, sort it and split it into O ⁡ ( T ) O(\sqrt{T}) groups of consecutive elements, each group of size O ⁡ ( n / T ) O(n/\sqrt{T}) . There are O ⁡ ( ( T ) 3 ) O((\sqrt{T})^{3}) triples of groups (one group per set), which we are going to call subinstances . Each solution triple lives in exactly one subinstance. However, by a standard argument [ 33 , 17 ] , there are only O ⁡ ( ( T ) 2 ) = O ⁡ ( T ) O((\sqrt{T})^{2})=O(T) nontrivial subinstances that may contain solutions, and they can be efficiently identified by examining the minimum and maximum elements in each group, and requiring that the sum of the three minimums is at most 0 0 and the sum of the three maximums is at least 0 0 . For ⌈ log ⁡ ( n / T ) ⌉ \lceil\log(n/\sqrt{T})\rceil rounds, repeat the following: Split the first set in each subinstance into two equisized parts, effectively doubling the number of subinstances. Run the decision algorithm on each subinstance 6 6 6 In order to run a decision algorithm for a one-set variant of 3SUM on three sets one can use the standard reduction between the two variants, see, e.g., [ 5 ] . and if it says “no”, discard this subinstance. At the end of the round, if the number of subinstances exceeds T T , discard arbitrarily chosen ones so that their count drops back to T T . After the last round, the first set in each subinstance is just a singleton, so all solutions in this subinstance can be listed by a linear scan in time O ⁡ ( n / T ) O(n/\sqrt{T}) , which is no more than the algorithm anyway spends in a single round. The correctness follows from the invariant that solutions coming from different subinstances are distinct, and that the total number of solutions across non-discarded subinstances is at least T T , or the total number of solutions was initially less than T T in which case the algorithm does not discard anything. The total running time of a single round is O ⁡ ( T ​ ( n / T ) 2 − ϵ ) = O ⁡ ( n 2 − ε ​ T ε / 2 ) O(T(n/\sqrt{T})^{2-\epsilon})=O(n^{2-\varepsilon}T^{\varepsilon/2}) , and there are O ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) O(\log n) rounds, which gives the claimed total running time. ∎

text: 3SUM Is Really Hard: A Real-to-Integer Reduction Skip to main content Report GitHub Issue × Title: Content selection saved. Describe the issue below: Description: Why HTML? Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.10153v1 [cs.DS] 07 Oct 2026 3SUM Is Really Hard: A Real-to-Integer Reduction Nick Fischer Affiliation: Max-Planck Institute for Informatics Adam Polak Affiliation: Bocconi University Jonas Schmidt Affiliation: Bocconi University Abstract We show that if the 3SUM problem on integer-valued inputs can be solved in truly subquadratic time, then it can also be solved in truly subquadratic time on real-valued inputs. This answers an open problem posed by Chan, Vassilevska Williams, and Xu [STOC 2022], and constitutes the first such tight real-to-integer self-reduction in fine-grained complexity. Our proof relies on a surprising combination of the Frank–Tardos theorem from optimization with Freiman-type theorems from additive combinatorics. 1 Introduction Given n n numbers, the 3SUM problem asks whether any three of them sum up to zero. It can be solved in time O ⁡ ( n 2 ) O(n^{2}) . One of the three main hypotheses of fine-grained complexity [ 39 ] , the 3SUM Hypothesis , asserts that this running time is optimal, up to subpolynomial n o ⁡ ( 1 ) n^{o(1)} factors. Some mild polylogarithmic improvements over the quadratic running time are however possible. In particular, Baran, Demaine and Pătra s , cu [ 2 ] showed that relatively simple hashing and bit-packing tricks suffice to obtain an O ⁡ ( n 2 log 2 ⁡ n ​ polyloglog ⁡ ( n ) ) O\big(\frac{n^{2}}{\log^{2}n}\polyloglog(n)\big) -time algorithm for Integer 3SUM, i.e., 3SUM with input numbers required to be integers. It took much more time and a series of papers [ 28 , 25 , 23 , 10 ] to arrive at the same running time also for real-valued inputs, and these Real 3SUM algorithms employ a significantly more complex approach based on linear decision trees. Gajentaan and Overmars [ 24 ] first introduced 3SUM in the context of conditional lower bounds for computational geometry problems, where it is natural to consider real-valued inputs. Later, Pătra s , cu [ 34 ] showed how to use hashing to reduce Integer 3SUM to combinatorial problems, such as finding triangles in graphs. This technique has quickly become prevalent in 3SUM-based hardness proofs (see [ 17 ] ), and in modern fine-grained complexity, 3SUM is essentially synonymous with Integer 3SUM. Chan, Vassilevska Williams, and Xu [ 7 ] asked whether fine-grained reductions from Integer 3SUM can be turned into reductions from Real 3SUM, and they made a partial progress on this question. In particular, they give non-tight reductions from Real 3SUM to the Integer All-Numbers 3SUM, All-Color-Pairs Triangle Collection, All-Edges Sparse Triangle, and All-Edges Monochromatic Triangle problems, as well as tight reductions to counting versions of the last two problems. They remark that “(…) it would be extremely interesting if one could show that the Real 3SUM hypothesis implies the Integer 3SUM hypothesis.” Our main result establishes this implication. 1.1 Real-to-Integer Reduction for 3SUM. If Integer 3SUM can be solved in time O ⁡ ( n 2 − ϵ ) O(n^{2-\epsilon}) , for some constant ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 , then Real 3SUM can be solved in time O ⁡ ( n 2 − Ω ⁡ ( ϵ 4 ) ) O(n^{2-\Omega(\epsilon^{4})}) (in the comparison-addition model). In other words, we show that Integer 3SUM is as hard as Real 3SUM. Thus, if we believe that Real 3SUM is really hard, then also Integer 3SUM and all the numerous problems with known (Integer) 3SUM-based fine-grained lower bounds are also really hard. We consider this result quite unexpected. To our knowledge, it constitutes the first and only tight real-to-integer self-reduction in fine-grained algorithms and complexity. Our result fits a broader line of work that tries to understand how much of the hashing-based machinery developed around 3SUM (and other related problems such as Subset Sum) is actually necessary. One part of this line deals with derandomization [ 5 , 17 ] , another (including this work) with real-valued inputs [ 7 , 19 ] . Further Consequences. Our reduction from Real to Integer 3SUM goes through an intermediate problem, the Real Convolution 3SUM problem, which asks, for a given input sequence a ∈ ℝ n a\in\mathbb{R}^{n} , to determine if there exist i , j , k i,j,k such that i + j = k i+j=k and a ⁡ [ i ] + a ⁡ [ j ] = a ⁡ [ k ] a[i]+a[j]=a[k] . The integer-valued version of this problem was first introduced by Pătra s , cu [ 34 ] , who showed that it is equivalent to Integer 3SUM under subquadratic fine-grained reductions, and used it as an intermediate problem for showing hardness of a number of combinatorial problems. Pătra s , cu’s reduction from 3SUM to Convolution 3SUM relies on linear hashing as in [ 2 ] —a technique inherently only suited to integers. It was later simplified and derandomized by Chan and He [ 5 ] , who “leave open the question of whether (…) a similar reduction from 3SUM to Convolution 3SUM is possible for real numbers.” We answer this question in the affirmative with our intermediate reduction ( Theorem 4.1 ). Another important problem in fine-grained complexity is the Exact Triangle problem, which asks to determine whether a given edge-weighted graph contains a triangle whose total edge weight equals exactly zero. In the world of integer-valued inputs, Exact Triangle is known to be harder than both 3SUM [ 41 ] and APSP [ 40 ] (All-Pairs Shortest Path, the second of the three central problems in fine-grained complexity), and thus its conjectured hardness gives rise to a weaker unifying hypothesis, which turns out to be sufficient to prove hardness of many problems previously known to be 3SUM-hard [ 42 , 9 ] . Up until now it was not known if there is a real analogue of the reduction from (Integer) 3SUM to (Integer) Exact Triangle. This reduction goes through the Convolution 3SUM problem and applies a generic convolution-to-product transformation [ 41 ] —the latter would work as well with real-valued inputs, but only our Theorem 4.1 establishes a real counterpart of the former. 1.2 . If Real Exact Triangle can be solved in time O ⁡ ( n 2 − ϵ ) O(n^{2-\epsilon}) , for some constant ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 , then Real 3SUM can be solved in time O ⁡ ( n 2 − Ω ⁡ ( ϵ 2 ) ) O(n^{2-\Omega(\epsilon^{2})}) (in the comparison-addition model). Another immediate consequence of our result is that all problems previously known to be as hard as Integer 3SUM (e.g., All-Pairs Sparse Triangle [ 34 , 31 ] ) are now also known to be as hard as Real 3SUM. 1.1 Computational Model In fine-grained complexity it is customary work in the word RAM model of computation with O ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) O(\log n) -bit words, which is a natural choice when the input consists of polynomially bounded integers. However, to deal with real-valued inputs, we need to move to a real RAM model with dedicated registers for storing real numbers and performing specific operations on them. Here we need to be particularly careful when describing the set of allowed operations on these real numbers, because reals are inherently infinite-precision and thus the model can easily gain unreasonable computational power. For instance, it is known that when supporting infinite-precision arithmetic operations and flooring allows solving PSPACE-complete problems in polynomial time [ 29 ] . But even without flooring, the real RAM model is unexpectedly powerful. The fine-grained complexity landscape would look very differently in that model; for instance, computing all-pairs shortest paths (in graphs with integer edge weights) is in truly subcubic time [ 44 ] . While 3SUM with real-valued input may still require quadratic time in such an unreasonably powerful computational model, we prefer to state our reductions in a model as weak as possible. It turns out that our reduction can be implemented in a very weak model, the comparison-addition model. This model, on top of the word RAM model, supports only two real-valued operations: comparisons ( a < b a<b ) and additions—no multiplication, no flooring, no logarithms. In fact, our reduction works in an even more restricted model which we will refer to as the realistic comparison-addition model. This model supports only a single operation, namely to evaluate a comparison of the form ∑ i = 1 m n i ​ α i ≥ 0 , \sum_{i=1}^{m}n_{i}\alpha_{i}\geq 0, where the n i n_{i} ’s are arbitrary non-zero integers and the α i \alpha_{i} ’s are input reals; each such operation is assumed to take time ( ∑ i = 1 m log ⁡ | n i | ) O ⁡ ( 1 ) (\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log|n_{i}|)^{O(1)} . 1 1 1 Note that we can still simulate additions in the realistic comparison-addition model, by performing all additions symbolically . Concretely, define a symbolic number as a tuple ( n 1 , … , n m , α 1 , … , α m ) (n_{1},\dots,n_{m},\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{m}) representing ∑ i = 1 m n i ​ α i \sum_{i=1}^{m}n_{i}\alpha_{i} , where the n i n_{i} ’s are integers and the α i \alpha_{i} ’s are pointers to the input reals. Two symbolic numbers can be added in time ( ∑ i = 1 m log ⁡ | n i | ) O ⁡ ( 1 ) (\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log|n_{i}|)^{O(1)} without invoking any operations on reals.
